## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. There exists a continuous function $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$, all of whose level sets have empty interior, that nevertheless has a level set of positive Lebesgue measure.

**Construction.** Let $C\subset[0,1]$ be the Smith–Volterra–Cantor (SVC) set. Recall that $C$ is obtained from $[0,1]$ by successively removing open middle intervals of lengths $\frac14,\frac1{16},\frac1{64},\dots$ (the $n$-th removal taking intervals of total length $\frac1{2^{2n}}$). The total removed length is
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{2n}}=\frac{1/4}{1-1/4}=\frac13,$$
so $C$ has Lebesgue measure $m(C)=1-\frac13=\frac23>0$. Being the complement (within $[0,1]$) of a countable union of open intervals, $C$ is closed; and since every removed interval is dense in the sense that the construction deletes an interval from every remaining interval at every stage, $C$ is nowhere dense, hence $\operatorname{int}(C)=\varnothing$.

Define
$$f(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=\inf\{|x-c|:c\in C\},\qquad x\in[0,1].$$

**$f$ is continuous.** The distance-to-a-closed-set function is $1$-Lipschitz: $|f(x)-f(y)|\le|x-y|$. Hence $f$ is (uniformly) continuous.

**The level set $f^{-1}(0)$ has positive measure.** Since $C$ is closed, $f(x)=0\iff x\in C$. Thus $f^{-1}(0)=C$, and
$$m\bigl(f^{-1}(0)\bigr)=m(C)=\tfrac23>0.$$

**Every level set has empty interior.** We check two cases.

*Level $t=0$:* $f^{-1}(0)=C$, which is nowhere dense, so $\operatorname{int}(f^{-1}(0))=\varnothing$.

*Level $t>0$:* The complement $[0,1]\setminus C=\bigcup_{k}(a_k,b_k)$ is a countable union of disjoint open intervals (the gaps removed during construction). On each gap $[a_k,b_k]$, the distance function satisfies
$$f(x)=\min\{x-a_k,\; b_k-x\},\qquad x\in[a_k,b_k],$$
since $a_k,b_k\in C$ are the nearest points of $C$ to $x$ within this gap. The equation $f(x)=t$ on $[a_k,b_k]$ has at most two solutions ($x=a_k+t$ and $x=b_k-t$, coinciding when $t=\frac{b_k-a_k}{2}$). Therefore
$$f^{-1}(t)\;\subseteq\;\bigcup_{k}\{a_k+t,\; b_k-t\},$$
a countable set. In particular $f^{-1}(t)$ is countable for every $t>0$, so it has empty interior (and measure zero).

Combining both cases, **every** level set $f^{-1}(t)$, $t\in\mathbb{R}$, has empty interior, yet $f^{-1}(0)=C$ has positive Lebesgue measure $\frac23$.

**Conclusion.** A continuous function on $[0,1]$ with no flat regions (all level sets having empty interior) can indeed possess a level set of positive Lebesgue measure. The key mechanism is that "empty interior" is a topological (Baire-category) condition strictly weaker than "measure zero": a nowhere-dense closed set such as the SVC set carries positive measure while having no interior, and the distance function to it realizes exactly this set as a level set while keeping all other level sets countable.
